title: Islamic finance today
hookLine: banks, mortgages and sukuk, and debates about them

cards: A couple sits across a desk from a bank officer, holding a printout of a house they love. The numbers are fine. Then one of them asks a question the officer may not hear every day: is there interest in this?

If there is, for them, the house may be off the table. That question has built a whole corner of modern banking, with its own mortgages, its own bonds, and its own arguments about whether it's done right.

teach.b: The root is a line in Surah al-Baqarah. Some people said trade is just like usury, and the Qur'an answers, in Pickthall: "Allah permitteth trading and forbiddeth usury." The Arabic for usury is riba.

In Sahih Muslim, Jabir reports that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, cursed the one who consumes riba, the one who pays it, the one who writes it down, and the two who witness it, and said they are all alike.
So trade is open; earning money purely from lending money is not. How do you buy a house, then? Islamic banks offer a few shapes.
In one, the bank buys the house and sells it to you at a known, fixed markup, paid over time. In another, the bank owns the house and you rent it until it's yours.
In a third, you and the bank buy it together as partners, and month by month you buy out the bank's share while paying rent on the part it still owns.

teach.h: SUKUK: OWNING PART OF AN ASSET.
teach.b: Bonds have a version too: sukuk, certificates of part-ownership in a real asset, where the return comes from that asset rather than from a loan. The debate is inside the tradition.

teach.h: REAL TRADE, OR A NEW NAME?
teach.b: Some scholars and critics say certain products are a conventional loan wearing an Arabic name: the monthly payment looks much the same.

Others answer that the form is the substance: the bank really owns something and really carries risk, so it's a trade, not a loan. Muslims who care about this weigh both, and come down in different places.

how: Muslims who avoid interest may use home financing from Islamic banks built on sale, lease or partnership, invest in sukuk, and consult scholars or Sharia boards on products, while some decide certain products are too close to conventional loans.

s: the Qur'an forbids trade and profit
Pickthall: "Allah permitteth trading and forbiddeth usury." trade is open.
in Sahih Muslim, the curse falls only on the one who consumes riba
Jabir reports it falls on the one who consumes it, the one who pays it, the one who writes it, and the two witnesses.
some scholars criticize certain Islamic finance products as loans with a new name
the debate is inside the tradition: form versus substance.

games.q: you want a home, and you won't pay interest. an Islamic bank offers to buy the house with you as partners. what happens next?
o: you pay interest on the bank's half.
you buy out the bank's share over time, paying rent on what it still owns.
the bank gives you the house as a gift.
games.why: in the partnership model, you buy the bank's share bit by bit, and pay rent on the part it still owns. critics say the payment can look much like a mortgage; defenders say real ownership changes it.

practice: Bring to mind one money arrangement in your life, a credit card, a car payment, rent, savings, and ask it three quiet questions: who owns what, who carries the risk, and where does the extra money come from? Just see it plainly.
If you pray, hold your earnings in mind as something you'll be asked about; if you don't, simply hold the three questions.

wordCard.voice: Islamic finance today. Banks, mortgages and sukuk built around one verse: trade is permitted, riba is forbidden, and the arguments over where one ends and the other begins. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the word Pickthall renders usury in 2:275.

carryVoice: Your line: finance without interest. Minorities, science, the body, the earth, the mosque, the plate, and now the wallet. Rest well.
